pulls.title: descriptor: compare x-only public keys in Tapscript Miniscript duplicate check
pulls.body:
In Tapscript Miniscript descriptors (`tr()`), public keys serialize as 32-byte x-only pubkeys per BIP-340, BIP-342, and BIP-379, discarding parity. However, `KeyParser::KeyCompare` in `src/script/descriptor.cpp` compared keys as full 33-byte `CPubKey`s, retaining the parity byte.

When a descriptor contains public keys that differ only in parity prefix (such as `pk(X)` alongside `pk(03X)` where `X` defaults to `02`, or `pk(02X)` alongside `pk(03X)`), `KeyParser::KeyCompare` treated them as distinct keys. Miniscript duplicate key checking passed, declaring the descriptor sane even though both branches serialize on-chain to `<X> OP_CHECKSIG`. Because a single signature satisfies both branches, third parties could malleate transactions by altering branch selectors without holding private keys, violating BIP-379 non-malleability invariants.

This patch updates `KeyParser::KeyCompare` in `src/script/descriptor.cpp` and `KeyConverter::KeyCompare` in `src/test/miniscript_tests.cpp` to compare keys as `XOnlyPubKey` whenever `miniscript::IsTapscript(m_script_ctx)` evaluates true. Under Tapscript context, keys sharing identical x-coordinates compare equivalent (`!comp(a, b) && !comp(b, a)`), ensuring `DuplicateKeyCheck()` detects the collision and rejects the descriptor. In `src/test/descriptor_tests.cpp`, unit tests verify that `tr()` descriptors containing parity-differing duplicate keys (including public hex and private WIF formats) are rejected as not sane, while `wsh()` descriptors continue to treat 33-byte compressed keys with differing parities as distinct.

Fixes #36414.

pulls.title: validation: fix false corruption errors after pruning or AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `getblockfrompeer` restores a pruned block's body without recreating its undo record. If startup verification reaches that block at level >2, it attempts to disconnect it and reports database corruption, preventing the node from restarting.

With ordinary pruning, reaching the restored block requires a deeper check than the default six blocks. The AssumeUTXO case can occur with the default checks.

**Fix:** Stop deep verification when a pruned node reaches missing undo data, using the existing result for unavailable history. The same allowance covers missing undo on AssumeUTXO snapshot chainstates, matching the existing treatment of unavailable snapshot history. Level 4 still reconnects the newer blocks that were disconnected. `verifychain` returns `false` to indicate incomplete verification, including when undo is missing at the snapshot base. Lower verification levels and corruption checks for undo records marked as present retain their existing behavior.

An AssumeUTXO restart can still hit a [separate block-index candidate assertion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36452#issuecomment-6464524112) after verification.

This came up during [pruned `txindex` review](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002). The pending `pruneassumevalid` change also needs verification to handle missing undo correctly, so this fix is being split out to land first.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc, gui: Allow users to manually rebroadcast a wallet transaction
pulls.body: From the discussion in #36403, it is clear that there needs to be a way for users to rebroadcast a transaction. Currently, the way to do so requires getting the raw transaction, getting the hex, and using `sendrawtransaction`. This PR adds `rebroadcastwallettx` RPC that takes a txid to attempt to rebroadcast that single transaction. An action is also added to the GUI menu for each transaction to do the same.

pulls.title: wallet: Only broadcast resubmitted transactions that were added to the mempool
pulls.body:
As discussed in #36403, one of the issues with current rebroadcast behavior is that the rebroadcast begins an unconditional relay of a transaction to peers. While this is broadcast is limited to peers that have not previously been inv'd the transaction, there is still a privacy leak in this double relay of a transaction, especially so for transactions that are still in nodes' mempools.

This PR changes the rebroadcast to only rebroadcast transactions if the transaction was not already present in our mempool. This provides some additional privacy while retaining intended rebroadcast behavior as transactions that have likely fallen out of nodes' mempools are the ones that actually need to be rebroadcast.

The wallet rebroadcast tests are additionally refactored for isolation so that their behaviors can still be tested after this change. Additionally, a test for the loading resubmission was added, as well as a test for the new behavior.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: reject duplicate coins and empty snapshot groups
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Snapshot loading doesn't validate the announced coin count against the unique UTXOs loaded.
Repeated outpoints collapse into one coin, so a snapshot can repeat every record, announce the doubled count, and still match the committed UTXO hash.
`loadtxoutset` then reports the inflated count as `coins_loaded`.

Snapshot loading also accepts transaction groups with no coins.
They leave the UTXO hash unchanged and don't advance the coin count, so parsing them bypasses the interrupt check and can delay shutdown.

**Fix:** Compare the announced count with the unique coin count already produced by the existing UTXO statistics scan, and reject zero-count transaction groups while parsing the snapshot.
When both the content hash and coin count are wrong, loading reports the hash error first.

pulls.title: rpc: reject AssumeUTXO rollback without tip data
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot on a pruned node can leave the active tip without block or undo data. Attempting a rollback with `dumptxoutset` then triggers an assertion and terminates the node.

**Fix:** Reuse `GetPruneHeight` to reject rollback with the existing pruning error when the required data is unavailable.

pulls.title: interfaces: Avoid node crashes from invalid Chain IPC calls
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A program using the `Chain` IPC interface from #29409 can crash `bitcoin-node` with a single bad call: asking for a block hash above the tip, passing a negative height to `hasBlocks`, leaving the transaction argument of `broadcastTransaction` or `checkChainLimits` unset, or returning an error from a notification handler. Separately, `findAncestorByHash` reports success when the descendant block is unknown (#36472). The `Chain` methods were written for in-process C++ callers like the wallet, which follow documented preconditions, so they assert or dereference null instead of returning errors.

**Solution:** Make these `Chain` methods in `src/node/interfaces.cpp` return errors for invalid arguments, catch and log IPC errors from notification handlers, and fix the `findAncestorByHash` check. Three small commits, each with unit tests in `src/test/interfaces_tests.cpp`. Valid calls behave the same as before. Details are in the commit messages.

This PR does not depend on #29409, but the fixes matter if it is merged and `interfaces::Chain` is exposed over IPC. The problems were reported by zaidmstrr, willcl-ark and xyzconstant while reviewing #29409, by enirox001 in #36472, and by cyb3ralbert and xyzconstant here (`hasBlocks`). The `findAncestorByHash` fix is the same one previously proposed by Romansage6 and Yudis-bit in #36473, #36484 and #36490.

Fixes #36472.

pulls.title: mining: add Block interface, fix template data race
pulls.body:
This PR catches two birds with one stone:

- fixes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36515
- adds a `Block` interface, which lets IPC clients fetch the block data (or its header)

This means a client can still fetch (and store) the block after `submitSolution()`, but we no longer mutate the template's `CBlock` for this.

### Block interface

`submitSolution()` no longer modifies the template. It applies the solution to a copy of the template block and returns a `Block` handle for that copy, also when the block is rejected.

`Mining::submitBlock()` and `BlockTemplate::block()` do the same. The new interface has a `data()`, `header()` and `coinbaseMerklePath()` method, so these are migrated from the `BlockTemplate` interface.

The interface can be expanded later, e.g. to tell whether the block is part of the active chain (or went stale, useful for a miner to know).

This is a breaking change for IPC clients:

- `getBlockHeader()` → `block().header()`
- `getBlock()` → `block().data()`
- `getCoinbaseMerklePath()` → `block().coinbaseMerklePath()`
- `bool submitSolution(..., reason, debug)` → `Block submitSolution(..., accepted, reason, debug)`
- `bool submitBlock(block, reason, debug)` → `Block submitBlock(block, accepted, reason, debug)`

It uses new ordinals and old methods throw.

`submitSolution()` now throws when the coinbase is null, instead of returning false.

### Performance

My agent measured how long after `submitSolution()` sv2-tp forwards the next template, with master as the baseline and an adapted sv2-tp as the client:

| Workload | Master | This PR | Paired median difference (95% CI) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Empty block | 1.32 ms | 1.40 ms | +0.05 ms [−0.11, +0.15] |
| Near-full block, 3.7 MB | 10.11 ms | 10.07 ms | −0.09 ms [−0.44, +0.28] |

The extra `block()` call costs about 0.15 ms per template for a C++ client. The alternative approach of having `submitSolution()` return the full `CBlock` added 6ms.

### Memory

A `Block` handle keeps the template's memory, including its transactions, allocated until the client destroys the handle. This also applies to handles returned by `submitSolution()` and `submitBlock()`. This doesn't matter much in practice since (the existing) clients don't hold on to a `Block` long.

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.


I analyzed the reason=expiry evictions from a 15-node monitoring fleet (data courtesy of b10c) and checked what happened to each transaction afterwards.

Across 938,157 unique expired transactions (2024-02-16 to 2026-10-21):

- 92.0% (863,451) were later mined; only 8.0% (74,706) never confirmed.
- At least 34% (316,381) show rebroadcast evidence, and 87% of those confirmed.
- Of the ones that confirm, half are mined within about 5 days of first expiry and 90% within about 55 days.

So time-based expiry is evicting transactions that get mined anyway, usually after a rebroadcast, it costs relay bandwidth.

See thread https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-how-many-mempool-transactions-are-evicted-by-time/132

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: allow retrying loadtxoutset after an interrupted load
pulls.body:
**Problem:** An interrupted `loadtxoutset` can leave an incomplete `chainstate_snapshot` database without its required `base_blockhash` marker. A later call can fail to open that database, requiring the operator to remove it manually before retrying.

**Fix:** Wipe the snapshot database before opening it so a later call can replace incomplete data. LevelDB acquires the database lock before deleting files, so a database held open by another load cannot be wiped. Also correct the startup warning to identify the missing marker and explain that retrying replaces the directory.

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block.
Log mismatches and raise a GUI/RPC warning while allowing IBD to continue.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** To send a `MSG_BLOCK` reply from disk, a node currently decodes the block and serializes it again without witnesses.
For `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK`, it already sends the stored bytes directly.
Serving `MSG_BLOCK` efficiently also matters for the proposed witnessless initial block download. [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476)

**Fix:** For `MSG_BLOCK` replies from disk on non-Signet chains, read the block into an owned byte buffer and check the header’s proof of work and expected hash.
Walk the serialized transactions directly and strip their witnesses in place.
Signet still uses `ReadBlock` to verify the Signet solution.
Header checks now run before transaction parsing, so if both the header and transaction data are corrupt, the node may log a different error.

**Performance:**
| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 3.204 ms | 0.369 ms | **8.7×** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 8.944 ms | 1.026 ms | **8.7×** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the path that sends witness blocks directly from disk. [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151)
Earlier work identified unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) · [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098)
The implementation also builds on bulk block reads. [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551)

pulls.title: psbt: analyzepsbt reports an error when outputs exceed inputs
pulls.body:
`AnalyzePSBT` computes `fee = in_amt - out_amt` once every input amount is known and returns it as is. A PSBT whose outputs are worth more than its inputs therefore gets a negative `fee` and a `next` role of updater, even though no wallet can ever sign it into a valid transaction. The function already returns `PSBT is not valid. ...` for bad input values, unspendable outputs and an out-of-range output total.

An output total above the input total is reported the same way:

```
before: {"fee": -1.00000000, "next": "updater", ...}
after:  {"next": "creator", "error": "PSBT is not valid. Output amount larger than input amount"}
```

The functional test builds a PSBT that spends a 1 BTC output into a 2 BTC output and checks the error and the `creator` role. Without the change the assertion on `next` fails. `rpc_psbt.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_multisig_descriptor_psbt.py`, `rpc_openrpc.py` and the psbt unit tests pass.

pulls.title: ipc: hold event loop references when using it in `CapnpProtocol`
pulls.body:
`EventLoop::loop()` exits when its reference count reaches zero. In `serve()` mode, the parent connection is the only reference keeping the loop running. Other `CapnpProtocol` methods called from threads not handling parent IPC requests do not hold their own references and therefore depend on the parent connection remaining alive.

Add `loopRef()` (code suggested by @ryanofsky in https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/376#discussion_r4268952676), which returns a new reference to the event loop or throws if the loop is not running or is shutting down, and use it in the methods that need the loop. Protect `m_loop` with a new `m_loop_mutex` to prevent `serve()` from destroying the loop while `loopRef()` is accessing it.

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: Improve loadtxoutset performance
pulls.body:
Significantly improves loadtxoutset performance via a number of changes:

 * parallel threads for decoding, hashing, serializing and writing to leveldb
 * no fsync() gating writes
 * no redundant loading into CoinsView
 
Also adds a subcommand to bitcoin-util for getting a snapshot's hash_serialized_3, muhash, coin count and total amount values without importing to leveldb first.

pulls.title: node: batch block file pruning in a single pass over block index
pulls.body:
When starting a node with pruning enabled (e.g. `-prune=550`) on a node with full chain history or pruning many files at once, `FindFilesToPrune` and `FindFilesToPruneManual` previously called `PruneOneBlockFile` once per file.

Because `PruneOneBlockFile` iterated over the entire `m_block_index` for each file, this was an O(M * N) operation (M = files to prune, N = total blocks). When pruning a full chain (~5,770 files and ~972k blocks), this triggered ~5.6 billion iterations and froze the node running on a Pi 5 for ~10 minutes on startup while holding `cs_main`.

This PR replaces `PruneOneBlockFile` with `PruneBlockFiles(const std::set<int>&)`, which collects all candidate files and prunes them in a single O(M + N) pass over `m_block_index` using a compact dynamic bitfield (`std::vector<bool>`). Also skips entries without block or undo data to avoid unneeded checks and prevent file 0 pruning from dirtying header-only or already-pruned index entries. The new signature is analogous to `UnlinkPrunedFiles({file_number});`.

Benchmarked with ~972k blocks and 5,770 files to prune:
- x86_64 (i7-8665U @ 1.90 GHz): 75.1s -> 14.7ms (~5,100x speedup)
- ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 5): 606.0s -> 26.3ms (>3,500x speedup)

Both timings were taken with a datadir whose block index and block file info records came from a full chain, with the `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files backfilled as 0-byte files. Pruning selection reads only the index and the file info, so empty files reproduce the startup cost without a full chain, and `UnlinkPrunedFiles` deletes them cheaply.

A case where this matters in practice is a pruned node restarting after a long outage. It downloads headers for the whole gap first, leaving many header-only entries behind, then has to prune a large backlog in a few flushes. The data-less skip avoids re-dirtying all of those entries, and the single pass bounds the work by the index size instead of files times index size.

Add unit test `blockmanager_prune_block_files_batch` to verify batch pruning, empty set no-ops, clean dirty-set behavior, and cleared block and undo metadata. Add a test for the `FindFilesToPruneManual` caller path, including a mixed valid and out-of-range file set. Update caller tests in `blockmanager_tests` and `rescan_tests`.

Addition, I ran the test on my laptop as well, going from full node to `prune=5000` took 8:11:
```
2026-11-11T16:50:09Z init message: Pruning blockstore…
2026-11-11T16:58:20Z block tree size = 975494
```

pulls.title: tracing: run USDT tests without BPF privileges
pulls.body:
The USDT functional tests currently use BCC to attach eBPF programs to Bitcoin Core’s tracepoints. This requires BCC, matching kernel headers, and elevated BPF permissions, making the tests awkward to run locally and
requiring a privileged container in CI.

Replace the BCC consumers with GDB. Each tested node runs as a debugger child, allowing the tests to enable the real USDT probes and inspect their arguments when execution reaches the probe location. This continues to test
the parts of the USDT interface provided by Bitcoin Core:

- the probe metadata is present and understood;
- the probes can be enabled and are reached in the expected scenarios; and
- their arguments have the expected values, sizes, and lifetimes.

All five tests can run with GDB and `binutils`, without BCC or matching kernel headers. The ASan CI job no longer needs a privileged container and uses `SYS_PTRACE` instead. This also removes the embedded BPF programs from
the tests, reducing their size and maintenance burden. Overall, the change removes roughly 660 lines of test and CI code.

#### Tradeoffs

- These tests no longer exercise the consumer-side eBPF path, including BCC   compilation, kernel BPF verification and loading, uprobe attachment, BPF-side argument decoding, and perf-buffer delivery. Problems confined to
  those components would no longer be detected here.
- LeakSanitizer is disabled for nodes run under GDB because it cannot operate under `ptrace`. Other sanitizer checks remain enabled.

The remaining coverage is focused on Bitcoin Core’s side of the USDT interface. Testing the general BCC, eBPF, and kernel uprobe is left to those consumers and the kernel.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Keys contain the six-byte script-hash prefix followed by a three-byte big-endian block height. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: fuzz: Add a target that feeds arbitrary bytes to V2Transport
pulls.body:
No fuzz target feeds V2Transport bytes that an honest peer would not send past the v2 key exchange. I add p2p_transport_v2_receive. It knows the transport's keys, builds the input from arbitrary bytes and from parts of a valid handshake (the peer key, garbage, the terminator, encrypted packets that may be corrupted, and runs of empty decoys that force a rekey), and feeds it in pieces of arbitrary size. Once the transport reports v2, it checks that its session id matches the peer's.

It reaches the v2 receive states and their failures, except the fallback to v1 and the wrong-magic disconnect, which need a v1 `version` header at the start of the stream; `p2p_transport_bidirectional_v1v2` reaches the first. 15 minutes with libFuzzer, ASan and UBSan found no crash.

pulls.title: descriptor, rpc, wallet: do not echo key material in error messages
pulls.body:
Some descriptor error messages quote the string the caller sent, and a descriptor can hold a private key. The error then carries the key, or part of it, into places the request may not go: an application's log, an error reporter, a screenshot shared for help.

This PR stops the quoting. A failing key is named by its position, a failing entry of `solving_data.descriptors` by its index, and a function name is quoted only where the parser accepts it. The commit message lists each changed error.

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `key '<key>' is not valid` | `key is not valid` |
| `Multi: key '<key>' is not valid` | `Multi: key 3: key is not valid` |
| `'wpkh(<key>)x' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Unexpected text after the closing ')' of wpkh()` |
| `'<start of a key>(<rest>' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Not a valid descriptor expression` |
| `Unable to parse descriptor '<descriptor>': Missing checksum` | `Unable to parse descriptor at index 1: Missing checksum` |
| `Could not add descriptor '<descriptor>': ...` | the same, quoting the public form of the descriptor |

pulls.title: bugfix: send shortened IPv6 addresses to SOCKS5 proxies in full
pulls.body:
Found while auditing #36628 

Already known upstream issue with C-tor: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/issues/32314

With `-proxy` pointed at Tor, outbound connections to IPv6 peers whose
 address contains an inner `::` always fail with "general failure".

 Core sends every SOCKS5 destination as a DOMAINNAME, with IPv6 in its
 compressed form. Tor copies the name into its relay BEGIN cell as
 `<name>:<port>`, and the exit's `tor_addr_port_split` first tries to parse
 the whole string as an IPv6 address. `2001:db8::1:8333` is a valid one,
 because the `::` absorbs the port as an eighth group. The exit then sees no
 port and closes the stream. Addresses written with all eight groups, or
 ending in `::`, are unaffected: appending `:port` to them does not give a
 valid address.

 About 20% of the IPv6 addresses in a gossip-filled addrman, and 29% of
 current IPv6 DNS seed answers, have an inner `::`. The failure is closed;
 there is no fallback to a direct connection.

 Note that this also effects private broadcast by default.

 This PR sends such addresses with all eight groups written out
 (`2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1`). `<name>:<port>` then has nine groups, so the exit
 splits at the last colon. Other forms:

 | Form                  | Tor         | Tor, SafeSocks 1 | getaddrinfo-based proxies |
 |-----------------------|-------------|------------------|---------------------------|
 | `2001:db8::1` (today) | fails       | fails            | works                     |
 | `[2001:db8::1]`       | works       | works            | fails                     |
 | ATYP IPv6             | works, logs a DNS-leak warning | refused | works         |
 | eight groups (this PR)| works       | works            | works                     |

 Tested against tor 0.4.9.13: on mainnet, master could not reach four
 seed-provided peers with inner-`::` addresses (30 "general failure"); with
 this change all four connected and completed the version handshake.
 `feature_proxy.py` and a new `netbase_tests` case check the bytes sent.

pulls.body:
`bitcoind` returns an useful error when invalid hex is passed to `-signetchallenge`:

pulls.title: validation: don't treat snapshot block as linked on startup
pulls.body:
Background sync requests blocks up to and including the snapshot block from several peers at once, so the snapshot block can be stored before one of its ancestors. `ReceivedBlockTransactions()` then keeps it in `m_blocks_unlinked`, but that isn't persisted. On restart `LoadBlockIndex()` gives it the hardcoded `m_chain_tx_count`, `PopulateBlockIndexCandidates()` makes it a background candidate, and `FindMostWorkChain()` walks back to its parent, which has no chain tx count:

```
Assertion failed: (pindexTest->HaveNumChainTxs() || pindexTest->nHeight == 0), function FindMostWorkChain, file validation.cpp, line 3217.
```

It needs a restart in that window, so it should be rare, but after that the node aborts on every start. The only ways out I found are `-reindex-chainstate` or `-reindex`, and both delete the snapshot chainstate.

Fix this by adding the snapshot block to `m_blocks_unlinked` on startup if an ancestor is missing, and not making it a background candidate until then. Both are needed, without the first one background validation stalls. A node that is already stuck starts with the fix and finishes background validation without a reindex.

The new step in `feature_assumeutxo.py` restarts the node after the snapshot block is submitted out of order, and fails on master. I also reproduced it over p2p with a test peer that withholds the snapshot block's parent.

These are the two changes from #35307 (closed, the motivation there was `submitblock` before `loadtxoutset`) without its blockfile and VerifyDB changes. cyb3ralbert hit the same assertion while testing #36452 (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36452#issuecomment-6464524112), which is still needed when the snapshot tip is at the snapshot block. #36149 drops the `BLOCK_HAVE_DATA` check in the branch right below, so whichever is merged second should match it.

With `add_to_wallet=false`, the returned hex is rejected by `testmempoolaccept`, and with `add_to_wallet=true`, `send` reports success, but the tx stays only in the wallet, not the mempool.

pulls.title: validation: delete pruned files after a failed flush
pulls.body:
If a flush that prunes block files fails before the block index write, the files are already marked pruned in memory, but `setFilesToPrune` is a local in `FlushStateToDisk()`. The next successful flush writes the pruned file info and never deletes the blk/rev files. Only `ScanAndUnlinkAlreadyPrunedFiles()` deletes them, at the next startup.

This is number 7 of ryanofsky's [post-merge review of #35714](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35714#pullrequestreview-5697890316). The block file flush failure from #35714 and the blocks directory `CheckDiskSpace()` failure both return before that write.

I worked on this because it lets me test my kernel pruning refactor (#36738, for #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111) against the issue he describes. The refactor moves the flush, block index write and file deletion that a pruning flush runs from `FlushStateToDisk()` into `WriteBlockStorage()`, and no unit test ran that sequence in prune mode. I rebased the refactor onto this branch, and the new tests pass on each of its commits.

The first three commits add tests that pass on master. The unit test fixtures apply `-prune` and `-fastprune` from `extra_args`, `chainstate_flush_failure_boundary` checks that a flush after a failed one writes what was skipped, and `prune_flush_failure` shows that a failed prune flush still leaves its files on disk after a retry.

The last commit keeps the selected files in `BlockManager` and deletes them after the next block index write. If that write fails they are dropped with the dirty entries, which means a file is only deleted once it is marked pruned on disk. Pending files don't force a write. The next flush that writes deletes them.

The disk-space failure and automatic pruning take the same path but have no test. Neither does the `FindNextBlockPos()` line that drops a file from the pending set when a block is written to it, which can happen after an assumeutxo snapshot validates.

pulls.title: refactor: move block writes and pruning into BlockManager
pulls.body:
`FlushStateToDisk()` handles block storage directly. It applies `BlockManager`'s prune locks, writes its pruned flag, checks its blocks directory space and runs the flush, index write and file deletion, while `BlockManager` reads the chainstate to pick files. A pruning API on block storage (#35627) would have to go through validation for all of it.

This moves the storage side into `BlockManager`, as described in the same issue. Validation decides which heights may be pruned and passes them as limits. `BlockManager` applies its prune locks, selects the files, flushes, writes the index and deletes the files, in the same order as before. There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

The kernel pruning functions in #36856 and #36857 use this.

Based on #36735 Draft until it is merged.

Thanks to musaHaruna for his [review on my fork](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#pullrequestreview-5533305792), which led to grouping and checking the prune limits and to moving the prune bookkeeping into `BlockManager`.

pulls.title: refactor: pass BlockManager to ChainstateManager
pulls.body:
`ChainstateManager` creates and owns its `BlockManager`, which means block storage can't exist without chainstate management. #35627 discussed moving that ownership out of `ChainstateManager`, and the kernel needs it to configure, read and prune block storage on its own.

`NodeContext` and the kernel now create the `BlockManager` first, pass it to `ChainstateManager` by reference and destroy `ChainstateManager` first.

The first commit makes the kernel's `ChainMan` destroy its `ChainstateManager` explicitly. On master `ChainMan` declares its context last, which destroys the context before the `ChainstateManager` that refers into it. Nothing reads through those references during teardown, so this changes no behavior, but the order no longer depends on how the members are declared.

The last commit removes `ChainstateLoadOptions::prune`. It duplicated the `BlockManager`'s prune mode, and the kernel never set it. Once the kernel can prune (#36856), that would make it refuse to reopen a data directory it had pruned.

The only behavior change to my knowledge is startup log order, because the block tree database opens before the script verification threads start.

An earlier version of this PR also moved `ImportBlocks` and replaced `BlockManager`'s friend declarations. I've taken them out as they're not relevant to this, but I think together better suited for a change that removes the `node/blockstorage -> validation` circular dependency (#36858)

The kernel side is #36854.

pulls.title: rpc: handle malformed jsonrpc 2.0 requests correctly
pulls.body:
While reviewing #36642 I found something else we missed in JSON-RPC 2.0:

If we receive a malformed request we would assume that we couldn't parse it's jsonrpc version and send an HTTP error.  This is how the legacy jsonrpc server worked (despite that behavior not ever being part of any ratified jsonrpc spec) and we maintain it as Bitcoin "legacy" jsonrpc protocol. However it's possible to form a request that does properly indicate jsonrpc 2.0 but is still malformed. In that case, we should not send an HTTP error: the correct protocol is to respond with `HTTP 200 OK` and include the jsonrpc error message in the response.

The solution is to check if we know the request's jsonrpc version before responding with an error.

We already correctly handle such malformed requests in batches and this is already tested in `test_batch_requests()` in `interface_rpc.py`

On master, the functional test in this PR actually crashes the node because the assumption is codified. Note that this crash requires:
1. RPC Authentication
2. A debug build

So this is not an urgent security fix, but a bug that might disrupt testing.

```
node0 stderr httprpc.cpp:46
    UniValue JSONErrorReply(UniValue, const JSONRPCRequest &, HTTPStatusCode &):
        'jreq.m_json_version != JSONRPCVersion::V2' check failed.
```


In release builds the node doesn't crash, but it returns HTTP 400 with a JSON-RPC 2.0 error body instead of HTTP 200.

pulls.title: wallet: fix crash when external signer wallet creation fails
pulls.body:
When testing a hardware wallet integration, I found that when attempting to create a wallet with the wrong app open on the hardware wallet, the GUI crashes instead of showing an error message. After restarting, when attempting to create a wallet with the same name again, it fails with "Database already exists". Over RPC, there's no crash, but `createwallet` returns error code -1 and leaves the same files and directories behind.

This happens when setting up an external-signer wallet. When the signer fails, setting up the wallet throws `std::runtime_error`, and `CreateWallet()` doesn't catch it. The GUI's worker thread has no handler, so the uncaught exception ends in `std::terminate`, and RPC's catch-all turns it into error code -1. The directory and `wallet.dat` are created before setup and never removed when setup fails.

This uncaught exception has been encountered previously in bitcoin-core/gui#395, and bitcoin-core/gui#396 stopped the dialog from enabling the "External signer" option, but didn't handle the exception.


Commit 1 catches the exception as `LoadWalletInternal()` does. The GUI shows an error dialog, and RPC returns error code -4, with the message starting with "Wallet creation failed."
Commit 2 ensures that on failure, it removes only what was created. It checks what exists with `fs::symlink_status()`, as `MakeDatabase()` does, so a `wallet.dat` symlink is kept even if its target doesn't exist, and it logs a warning when a removal fails. The cleanup also runs for failures that don't throw, e.g. an invalid `-addresstype`.
Commit 3 adds a release note.

How to reproduce:
```
cmake -B build -DBUILD_GUI=ON && cmake --build build
build/bin/bitcoin-qt -regtest -datadir=$(mktemp -d) -signer="python3 test/functional/mocks/invalid_signer.py"
```


Then click File, Create Wallet, Create. "External signer" is already ticked and the name is pre-filled as `trezor_t`.

On master: `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'`, the process aborts, and `trezor_t/wallet.dat` is left behind.
With the PR: a "Create wallet failed" dialog appears, a retry shows the same dialog, and nothing is left on disk.

The tests `CreateWalletSignerFailure` and `CreateWalletInvalidArgs` in `wallet_tests` create wallets through the wallet loader, which is the same call the GUI makes. `wallet_signer.py` now expects -4, and checks that a failed creation leaves nothing behind, that a retry fails the same way, and that a directory, files or a dangling `wallet.dat` symlink that already existed are kept; in the symlink case the database created at the link's target stays too, and the check is skipped on Windows, as in `wallet_multiwallet.py`. An empty `wallet.dat` that already existed is initialized by the attempt and kept, so the name is taken afterwards, as before this PR.

You can see the tests fail without the fix:

```
git checkout HEAD~3 -- src/wallet/wallet.cpp
cmake --build build
build/bin/test_bitcoin --run_test=wallet_tests/CreateWalletSignerFailure,CreateWalletInvalidArgs
build/test/functional/wallet_signer.py
```

pulls.title: kernel: Dispatch log callbacks with btcsignals
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A kernel application whose log callback logs, or destroys a kernel object, hangs. The common way to hit this is a garbage-collected language binding: Python's garbage collector can run finalizers inside the callback, and a finalizer that destroys a chainstate manager flushes and logs (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34775#issuecomment-6278257737, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4030551866). The cause is that the kernel calls log callbacks while holding the logger's mutex, so any logging from inside a callback blocks on a mutex its own thread already holds. The problem is not new and has existed since logging callbacks were introduced in #30595.

**Solution:** This PR delivers log entries through `btcsignals::signal`, which calls callbacks without holding any lock, replacing the kernel's own callback list and custom dispatching mechanism.

The change is a usability improvement and a bugfix because with it applications no longer need to reason about deadlocks and blocking behavior from a mutex they can't see. However, they may need to be updated to deal with log callbacks that are no longer serialized and connection functions that no longer block. Compatibility details are in the commit message.

The main code change is in `src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.cpp` (+42/-77) accompanied by header docs and new test_kernel cases, which hang without the fix. There is also a commit switching `btcsignals.h` to use `StdMutex` instead of `Mutex` so it is safe to use in logging callbacks.

This is an alternative to the last commit of #34775, which fixes the same deadlock but only after limiting the process to one logging connection, and still hangs if a callback destroys the connection.

pulls.title: bip352: match P2SH-P2WPKH instead of evaluating it
pulls.body:
For P2SH inputs, `GetPubKeyFromInput` evaluated the full scriptSig with `EvalScript` and then ran `Solver` on the redeem script, even though only P2SH-P2WPKH is eligible for BIP-352. That costs time on every non-segwit P2SH spend (e.g. multisig), whose scriptSigs can be up to `MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE`.

BIP-141 requires the scriptSig of a P2SH-wrapped witness program to be exactly a single push of the redeem script (`SCRIPT_ERR_WITNESS_MALLEATED_P2SH`). So any valid P2SH-P2WPKH scriptSig is exactly `0x16 OP_0 0x14 <20-byte keyhash>`, and matching that template gives the same result without evaluating anything.

### Benchmarks

`bench_bitcoin -filter='BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_.*' -min-time=2000`, Release build.

Before:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|              688.30 |        1,452,858.07 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            7,158.19 |          139,700.11 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

After:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|               56.87 |       17,584,611.40 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            6,949.45 |          143,896.18 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

P2SH multisig is about 12x faster to rule out. P2SH-P2WPKH saves about 200 ns per input; its time is still dominated by `CPubKey::IsFullyValid()`.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.
Require a receiver that has not advanced beyond genesis, already knows the snapshot base header and has no stored blocks beyond genesis or unfinished reindexing.
This removes runtime activation checks, temporary import cache resizing and service demotion while preserving snapshot validation, resumption and background validation.

pulls.title: net: Automatically detect IPv4 and IPv6 reachability
pulls.body:
In many network environments, IPv6 peers cannot be reached, which is currently not detected. As a result, IPv6 addresses take up spots in AddrMan, and we make futile attempts to connect to them (e.g. feelers or network-specific connections). The reverse (IPv6 is reachable, but IPv4 isn't) is much rarer, but also possible.

This PR introduces an automatic check for IPv4/IPv6 reachability. The idea is to `connect()` a UDP socket to several well-known global unicast addresses. Because it's UDP, this only performs a local route lookup and source address selection, so no packets are sent out. Depending on specific error codes (e.g. `ENETUNREACH`), or if the selected source address is unusable (link-local, loopback), we decide that a network has no route. This is done conservatively to avoid false positives: in case of inconclusive evidence, the network stays reachable.

If the check finds no route for either IPv4 or IPv6 (but not both, because then we most likely have no connectivity at all), the network is marked as unreachable. This means we won't make automatic outbound connections to it, won't add new addresses from it to AddrMan, and relay its addresses slightly less. The first check runs one minute after startup rather than immediately, so that short gaps at startup (e.g. addresses still being configured) don't cause us to drop anchors or fixed seeds. After that, the check is repeated every 10 minutes, so the node can adapt to changing network conditions.

The check is disabled by any `-onlynet` setting, for networks reached through a proxy, and if automatic outbound connections are disabled (`-connect`). 

This is related to #35750, which addresses the same problem from the AddrMan side (not counting failures on networks we can't reach).

I'll keep this PR in draft for a while, until I have more confidence that the check works on various systems and has no false positives. I also haven't explored the possibility of unit/functional tests for it yet.

Test reports are very welcome, especially from more uncommon setups (e.g. IPv6-only, NAT64, containers, VPNs, Windows/BSD). Running with `-debug=net` shows the reason for each decision.

pulls.title: fuzz: report more events, and check more invariants in connman target
pulls.body:
On top of #36765, this extends FuzzedSock to report more events a real OS could report (see #36737 for some coverage of those), and improves the connman fuzz target to assert more socket handling invariants.

The first commit is also a fix to uniquely identify sockets, as currently each socket can only use one of two descriptor values, which means the fuzz target would act on one peer with the event of another.

See commit messages for details.

pulls.title: cmpctblock: Cache serialized cmpctblock msg for relay [part of prefill series]
pulls.body:
This PR extends the optimization added in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23880 which applies to peers that have requested HB blocks from us to also cache the serialized blocks for low-bandwidth peers. The core change here comes from the closed #26755 made by andrewtoth, but also includes other refactors and type safety improvements.

Performance is less critical for low-bandwidth peers, so this change on its own should have little impact on block propagation, but these refactors are useful as part of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35558 which adds prefilling of compact blocks, and where we run the risk of potentially having to serialize more than one cmpctblock_msg (one prefilled and one not-prefilled).

pulls.title: p2p: ignore historical blocks when counting blocks in flight
pulls.body:
While background validation runs after loading an assumeutxo
snapshot, blocks needed only by the background (historical) chainstate
are also tracked in mapBlocksInFlight. The condition that decides
whether a new block is requested as a compact block counted those
blocks as well, so with historical blocks in flight the new block at
the tip was requested as a full block instead.

Do not count blocks that are only needed by the historical chainstate.
Compact block relay then works normally during background validation.

Behavior is unchanged when no snapshot is loaded, because in that case
there are no historical blocks to exclude.

pulls.title: validation: avoid partial override of non-valid validation state
pulls.body:
ValidationState::Error() only sets the reject reason if the state is still valid. When it is called on a state that is already Invalid or Error, the mode changes but the earlier reason, result and debug message are kept. The result is a mix of the old and new error. Code review in #35570 found two places where this happens. This makes the in-and-out use of the state parameter harder to follow and to remove later.

This PR makes both cases explicit:

1. `ConnectBlock()` → `CheckBlock()` with a mutated block (`BLOCK_MUTATED`, e.g. a merkle root mismatch). This is treated as a sign of corruption and reported through `FatalError()`, but the resulting Error state kept `BLOCK_MUTATED` / `bad-txnmrklroot`. Now the Invalid state is logged and then replaced, so the Error state carries the corruption message.

2. `ActivateBestChainStep()` → `DisconnectTip()` → `FlushStateToDisk()` failure. `FlushStateToDisk()` has already reported a fatal error, and `ActivateBestChainStep()` then called `FatalError()` a second time with a less specific message. Now the existing error is logged and returned unchanged, and no second fatal error is reported.

Behavior changes:

- Case 1: the returned state has the reject reason "Corrupt block found indicating potential hardware failure.", no result and no debug message. The original reason is logged.
- Case 2: the duplicate fatal-error notification is no longer sent. The returned reject reason does not change.

The first commit adds a unit test for case 1 that captures the current behavior, and the second commit updates its expectations. Case 2 has no test, because a flush failure cannot be triggered without fault injection. The path where `DisconnectTip()` fails while the state is still valid is covered by `feature_abortnode.py` and is unchanged.

pulls.title: test: make script_combineSigs and spends_witness_prog cases independent
pulls.body:
Part of #36692: remove test state that is shared and modified across cases.

- `script_combineSigs`: The P2PKH, P2SH and multisig cases shared one funding transaction, whose `scriptPubkey` was modified between them, and one keystore. Each case is now its own test with its own keys, keystore and funding transaction.
- `spends_witness_prog`: every output type reused the same transactions and coins view. The P2SH-wrapped cases relied on the `scriptPubkey` left by the previous case and had to clear the `scriptSig` they set. Each check now builds fresh state, and the scripts are named.

The checks are unchanged.

pulls.title: wallet, sqlite: Enable secure_delete by default
pulls.body:
Currently, when we make deletions or updates to the database that require records to be fully deleted and to not persist in free pages afterwards, we need to explicitly call `WalletDatabase::Rewrite`. This behavior was introduced in #635 to ensure that unencrypted private keys are erased from the database after encrypting a wallet, and initial encryption is the only consumer of this function.

However, initial encryption is not the only functionality that requires secure deletion. l0rinc's LLMs recently found changing the passphrase can leave the original that encryption key record in free pages. We should want to ensure that those records are also deleted, although I do not consider that the presence of such records in free space to actually be a problem. Note that this behavior appears to be present since wallet encryption was initially introduced in #352.

Fortunately, SQLite offers a secure_delete flag that can be enabled on each connection to a database. If set, all deletes or updates will ensure that any data that was deleted or overwritten actually are overwritten with 0's. It is one of the 2 methods in SQLite's documentation for ensuring that records do not persist in free pages, the other method being to call `VACUUM` after deletions or updates, which is what `Rewrite` does.

The downside is that secure_delete will increase CPU and disk I/O, which is why this was not set previously. However, it seems like several distros ship with secure_delete enabled by default: [Debian](https://sources.debian.org/src/sqlite3/3.54.1-2/debian/rules#L48#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Ubuntu](https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/sqlite3/plain/debian/rules#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Fedora](https://src.fedoraproject.org/rpms/sqlite/raw/rawhide/f/sqlite.spec#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE=1), [Arch](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/sqlite/-/raw/main/PKGBUILD#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), and [NixOS](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/pkgs/development/libraries/sqlite/default.nix#L184) all set SQLite's compile time option to default secure_delete to enabled, and these are just the ones I've looked at. This suggests to me that the performance penalty is not actually that bad. As I run Arch and often do not use depends builds, I had not noticed that secure_delete was always on and did not experience any particularly poor wallet performance that could be attributed to that behavior. In the grand scheme of things, erases and updates are fairly infrequent in the wallet.

This PR enables secure_delete when the database is opened, and also enables it by default in the sqlite depends package. There are also a couple tests to check that all records we want deleted actually are being deleted from the database. `WalletDatabase::Rewrite` is removed as it it is no longer used.

pulls.title: test: construct fee estimator test transactions declaratively
pulls.body:
Part of #36692. 

`blockpolicyestimator_tests`: Replace the transaction template, whose `prevout` index was overwritten to make each `txid` unique, with `make_tx()`, which constructs each transaction with `COutPoint`, `CTxIn` and `CTxOut` constructor calls.

Move the code that submits a transaction to the estimator, which was repeated in three places, into `add_tx()`. Each transaction is now built once and shared between its mempool entry and the estimator. The transactions submitted to the estimator and its estimates are unchanged.

`mempool_fee_estimator_tests`: Construct the input and output of `MakeRandomTx()` in place instead of resizing the vectors and assigning each field afterwards. Apart from the random `prevout` hash, the transaction is identical to before.

pulls.body:
This PR continues the ongoing effort to enforce IWYU warnings.

See [Developer Notes](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/developer-notes.md#using-iwyu).

pulls.title: crypto: copy HMAC state instead of rehashing key pads
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Setting up an encrypted connection derives six values with the same secret. Each HKDF expansion repeats two SHA256 compressions to hash the same HMAC key pads.

**Fix:** Hash the key pads once per HKDF context, then copy the prepared HMAC state for each expansion. The copy replaces two setup compressions, saving ten SHA256 compressions across the six outputs - the derived bytes stay identical. [RFC 2104 section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104.html#section-4) describes this optimization:

> the intermediate results … on the B-byte blocks (K XOR ipad) and (K XOR opad) can be precomputed only once

**Measurements:**

```text
BIP324_HKDF (ops/s, higher is better)
Before  █████████████████████████████████░░░░░░░  1,430,064  (baseline)
After   ████████████████████████████████████████  1,724,373  (+20.6%)
```

pulls.title: refactor: remove more dead code
pulls.body: Similar to #36509. Also generally related to #36167.

pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps reply lines at 16 characters. As a result, most success paths can't be reached, and the code that parses the control port (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) never runs.

This rewrites the target around a fake Tor on the other end of a real `TorControlConnection`, connected through `DynSock`. Replies go over the wire. The fake Tor answers each command the controller sends with a reply of the matching shape, so inputs can complete the whole handshake: PROTOCOLINFO, authentication (including SAFECOOKIE), GETINFO and ADD_ONION. The harness also checks that reply data never splits a command or injects a new one.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`, which deleted its own socket. The bug has been there since #30205; this target is the first caller.

### Testing

Line coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp` goes from 52% on master to 81% after a 10-minute local run. The master number is from the qa-assets corpus. Most of what remains is the controller thread itself, which the harness replaces, and socket errors that `DynSock` can't produce.

The input format changes, so the corpus in qa-assets needs a refresh.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Skip legacy wallet records rather than erasing them, and drop unused record erase functions
pulls.body: When migrating a legacy wallet, we can skip the records in `MigrateToSQLite` that we would delete later on during migration. These records are specifically all of the legacy wallet records, and transaction records. The legacy wallet records are replaced with descriptor records produced during migration, and transaction records are already being rewritten by migration, so not writing them in the first place is also fine. This allows us to remove several database record erase functions, specifically EraseTx and EraseRecords.

pulls.title: rpc: Return the right RPCErrorCode more consistently
pulls.body:
Currently, rpc code may return the wrong `RPCErrorCode`. This is perfectly fine, because they should be hit rarely in production.

However, it could be good to be self-consistent. (Otherwise, we could just remove the different error codes and return a single one)

So fix a few error codes:

* An integral out-of-range is now `RPC_TYPE_ERROR`, not `RPC_MISC_ERROR`
* Some invalid args are now `RPC_INVALID_PARAMETER`
* Some transient issues or user-config issues are now `RPC_MISC_ERROR`

pulls.title: test: Kill validation mutants
test: split `CreateNewBlock_validity` into independent test cases
pulls.body:
`CreateNewBlock_validity` mines a 110-block chain and then runs four subtests on it as member functions. The subtests share one chain, so each starts from whatever the previous one left behind, and the caller has to patch `Tip()->nHeight` between them. Inside `TestBasicMining` a single `CMutableTransaction` is reused across all sections, with each section overwriting some of its fields, so the transaction a section actually tests depends on every section before it.

This PR removes both kinds of hidden state.

pulls.title: kernel: let callers create the block manager
pulls.body:
The kernel creates its block storage inside `btck_chainstate_manager_create`, configures it through the chainstate manager's options and reads blocks through the chainstate manager. Pruning (#35627) needs block storage that the caller can configure, keep and prune directly.

This adds `btck_BlockManagerOptions` and `btck_BlockManager`. `btck_chainstate_manager_create` takes a block manager and keeps a shared reference to it, so either handle can be destroyed first. A block manager can be passed to only one chainstate manager, and a failed creation still uses it up unless the contexts differ. `btck_block_read` and `btck_block_spent_outputs_read` take the block manager, and block tree entries are valid for its lifetime, which can be longer than the chainstate manager's.

Changes for callers:
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_create` no longer takes a blocks directory.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_wipe_dbs` is replaced by `btck_block_manager_options_update_wipe_block_tree_db` and `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_wipe_chainstate_db`. The block tree db is wiped when the block manager is created, and wiping it also wipes the chainstate db, which the old function required anyway.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_block_tree_db_in_memory` moves to the block manager options.
- Both options objects take the same total database cache, and each uses its own share.

Based on #36739. Draft until it is merged. Feedback on the API is welcome in the meantime.

pulls.title: kernel: add manual pruning
pulls.body:
Part of #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111. The kernel can't open a data directory that a pruned node created, and it has no way to prune.

This adds a prune option on the block manager, `btck_block_manager_prune_up_to_height` and `btck_chainstate_manager_flush`. With the option set, the kernel opens pruned data directories. The chainstate manager created with the block manager decides what may be deleted, so pruning fails without one.

Pruning writes only block storage, never the chainstate. After an unclean shutdown the chainstate on disk is at the last flush, and recovering from there needs the blocks above it. Pruning therefore keeps every block above the fork point between the last flushed block and the active chain, and reports `btck_PruneStatus_NEEDS_FLUSH` when that bound limited what it could delete. The caller can flush and prune again.

The fork point matters when the flushed block was reorged out. Recovery then disconnects the stale blocks, which needs their block and undo data, and connects the new ones from their block data. `btck_block_manager_prune_reorg_tests` covers that case and fails if the bound uses the flushed block's height instead.

A fast prune option lets tests prune, since test chains never fill a 128 MiB block file.

Based on #36738 and #36854. Draft until both are merged.

pulls.title: refactor: break the blockstorage/validation circular dependency
pulls.body:
`node/blockstorage.cpp` includes `validation.h`, and the lint lists `node/blockstorage -> validation -> node/blockstorage` as an expected circular dependency. This removes it, and the lint confirms the cycle is gone.

The largest user of validation in block storage is `ImportBlocks`, which drives validation. It moves to `node/chainstate` and sets the reindex flag through the new `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()`, which writes the flag to the block tree database and sets the in-memory flag under one `cs_main` hold. The last commit moves `FatalError` to `kernel/fatal_error.h`, after which `blockstorage.cpp` no longer includes `validation.h`. `validation.h` still exports `FatalError` for its other users.

Validation also reaches into `BlockManager`'s private members as a friend. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping `m_check_for_pruning` and `m_dirty_blockindex` non-public. Both require `cs_main`, and the annotations let the compiler check it. After this, nothing outside `BlockManager` writes its private state or the block tree database.

There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36738. Draft until it is merged.

Thanks to musaHaruna, who [suggested `RequestPrune()`](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#discussion_r4283138022) in his review on my fork. The flag marks a pending pruning check, so callers request it and storage decides whether anything qualifies, which keeps the flag private once the friend declarations are gone.

pulls.title: wallet: guard null coin control in AvailableCoins TRUC filter
pulls.body:
AvailableCoins() takes an optional CCoinControl pointer that defaults to nullptr, and the other uses of it check for null first. The TRUC version filter added in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/ec2676becdf488f7a1151345a019c05dec926308 does not, so a call without coin control dereferences a null pointer as soon as the wallet has an unconfirmed output in the mempool.

Found this issue with few seconds of fuzzing with the change in the second commit which adds wallet transactions in the mempool state with a fuzzed version, and call `AvailableCoins()` directly with an optional null coin control.

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric options were read with GetArg<int>() and then stored into unsigned or wider members without a range check. A negative value wrapped to a huge value and disabled the limit it was meant to configure, and a value wider than the destination could silently become a different number.

Parse the options whose destination is unsigned with ToIntegral<T>() on the raw string rather than with GetArg<T>(): the typed getter saturates values it cannot represent (so a leading '-' for an unsigned T becomes 0), while ToIntegral rejects '-', trailing garbage and overflow instead of saturating. Reject the remaining out-of-range values where they are read:

- -maxtipage: uint32_t seconds, range [0, UINT32_MAX]. A negative age placed the IBD cutoff in the future, so the node never treated its tip as recent.
- -dbbatchsize: uint64_t bytes. A negative value wrapped to a huge batch size and disabled flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch.
- -dbcrashratio: uint32_t, range [0, UINT32_MAX]. CoinsViewOptions::simulate_crash_ratio is changed from int to uint32_t to match.
- -limitclustercount: [1, MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT_LIMIT]. The separate upper-bound check in ApplyArgsManOptions is folded into this one, so an invalid value is reported once with one message.
- -limitclustersize: [1, INT64_MAX / 1000] kB. Zero made every transaction exceed the cluster size and blocked all mempool admission.
- -limitancestorcount, -limitdescendantcount: non-negative.
- -mempoolexpiry: [0, std::chrono::seconds::max() / 3600] hours, and the value is stored as seconds directly. The bound is taken from seconds rather than hours because std::chrono::hours is not guaranteed to be 64-bit.
- -datacarriersize: [0, UINT_MAX]; still unchecked when -datacarrier=0 turns the limit off.
- -bytespersigop: [0, UINT_MAX]. A negative value wrapped and inflated the sigop-adjusted size of every transaction until all were non-standard.
- -maxsendbuffer, -maxreceivebuffer: [0, UINT_MAX / 1000], since both are multiplied by 1000 into unsigned int members.
- -bantime: greater than 0. Zero or negative made setban without an explicit duration create an already expired ban.
- -timeout: positive and at most INT_MAX milliseconds. A non-positive value now fails instead of silently falling back to the default (as -peertimeout already did), and a value above INT_MAX used to narrow before it could be checked (e.g. 2^32 + 1 became 1).
- -txconfirmtarget: [1, UINT_MAX] in parameter interaction, and additionally bounded by the fee estimator's maximum when a wallet is loaded. A target beyond the estimator's range made every transaction fall back to -fallbackfee. The help text now states the minimum.

Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": -dbbatchsize, -datacarriersize, -mempoolexpiry, -maxtipage, -bytespersigop, -maxsendbuffer, -maxreceivebuffer, -limitancestorcount and -limitdescendantcount.

Since -nofoo is parsed as 0, add DISALLOW_NEGATION to the options where 0 is valid but very different from "no limit": -dbbatchsize, -mempoolexpiry, -maxreceivebuffer, -maxsendbuffer, -maxtipage, -limitancestorcount, -limitdescendantcount and -datacarriersize. Options that already reject (-bantime, -timeout, -peertimeout, -limitclustercount, -limitclustersize, -txconfirmtarget) need no separate check: negation reports the value error once. -bytespersigop still allows negation, because 0 turns the sigop adjustment off, which is exactly what -nobytespersigop says.

ReadCoinsViewArgs now returns util::Result<void> (marked [[nodiscard]]) so its errors abort startup instead of being discarded.

Finally, -help gains the =<n> placeholder for the options that take a value (-dbbatchsize, -bytespersigop, -datacarriersize, -stopatheight, -checkblockindex) and states the bounds for -bantime, -limitclustercount, -limitclustersize and -txconfirmtarget.

Add unit tests for the option parsers and functional tests for the accepted, rejected and negated forms.

pulls.title: mining: use steady clock for waitNext timeout
pulls.body:
Follow up suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36791#discussion_r4568050151.

`waitNext` measures its timeout and 1-second fee tick with the wall clock, while `waitTipChanged` uses the steady clock. This means a wall clock jump changes how long `waitNext` waits, and it never times out while mocktime is frozen.

Use the steady clock for the deadline and tick. `NodeClock` is kept only for the testnet 20-minute rule, which must compare node time with the tip's timestamp.

pulls.title: wallet: Clear streams before advancing BDB cursor
pulls.body:
This fixes a case where migratewallet can reject an old wallet as corrupt, i.e. this occurs on wallets used in Bitcoin Knots. The v2 key metadata may include an extra flag byte that Core’s metadata loader leaves unread. 

LoadRecords reuses its key and value streams between records. BerkeleyROCursor::Next() appends to those streams, so unread bytes from one record become part of the next and can cause a deserialization error.

Clear both streams before copying the next record, matching SQLiteCursor::Next(). This keeps the existing metadata parsing and migration code.

The regression test reads two records while leaving part of the first key and value unread, then checks that the second record replaces both outputs.

Testing on Linux:
- Without the fix, the regression fails both stream-content checks.
- With the fix, test_bitcoin --run_test=db_tests passes all tests

pulls.title: test: cover scantxoutset scan-object validation errors
pulls.body: The existing tests cover invalid range values but miss a few cases where the scan object itself is malformed. This adds three checks for when the scan object is not a string or object, when `desc` is missing, and when `range` has an invalid format. Each case verifies that the RPC returns the expected error (-8).

pulls.title: init: Fix surprising behaviors of negated options
pulls.body:
While looking into #36759 I discovered `-notorcontrol` did the opposite of what would be expected from it and I then checked for similar issues in other init options. There are several more where `-nofoo` does something surprising including one of them crashing the node.

This PR attempts to fix all these surprising behaviors while also keeping things as simple as possible and just change behavior to something that makes sense harmless in the context of the option. Fixes that use a common approach for the fix are grouped together into a commit even if the options included themselves may have no relation at all.

| Commit | Problematic options behavior | Fix approach |
|---|---|---|
| [mempool: Reject cluster limits below 1](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/512773d111daaa4330c873ed5889b9ef511f6e3a) | `-nolimitclustercount` hits an assertion in `TxGraph` on the first mempool transaction. `-nolimitclustersize` rejects every transaction. | Reject values below 1 at startup. |
| [args: Add NEGATE_TO_EMPTY so -nofoo reads as an empty string](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/ac4b8feb3fe151d1b00085cfe15a856ccede6e6e) | `GetArg()` returns `"0"` for a negated option. The `-no*notify` options run the command `0`, `-nosigner` uses `0` as signer, `-noi2psam` fails startup and `-norpcpassword` sets the password to `0`. Opt-in because options like `-noonion` and `-noblockfilterindex` depend on reading `"0"`. | New opt-in flag `NEGATE_TO_EMPTY` makes `GetArg()` return `""`. |
