pulls.title: net, http: handle socket errors separately from reads
pulls.body:
On Linux a socket error or hangup is reported whether or not we asked for it. If that happens for a peer we did not request to read from, disconnect directly. This just adds clarity: previously we would attempt a send that would then fail. The only side-effect is a changed log message. Nothing changes on other platforms: since bitcoin/bitcoin#36716 they no longer report errors for established connections.

The last commit does the same for HTTP, where on error it also no longer attempts a final read from a client whose reads are paused.

As a followup to bitcoin/bitcoin#36716, `p2p_socket_errors.py` adds coverage for existing behavior:
- the node ignores a single urgent byte: the connection stays open, ordinary data is still processed and the urgent byte is not counted as received.
- a peer resets the connection while the node's send to it is stalled and receiving from it is paused: the node disconnects without reading anything more (the change above only changes the log message)

Similarly `interface_http.py` checks that:
- a single urgent byte does not disturb an ordinary request.
- a client reset while the server has unsent responses (the HTTP change only changes the log message)

The first commit drops a comment from the `wait_ignores_urgent_data` unit test, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#discussion_r4700726004.

To support the new tests, the test framework gains:
- `wait_for_send_stall()`, moved out of `p2p_ping_ibd.py`
- a `reset` option for `peer_disconnect()`, which closes the connection with a TCP reset
- `mine_large_block()` returns the block hash and size
- `pack_linger()`, and `linux_host` / `windows_target` to tell which log message to expect

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: blockstorage: lock blocksdir in BlockManager
pulls.body:
While playing around with pruning for the kernel, I noticed that only bitcoind's init locks the blocks directory (`AppInitLockDirectories`). The kernel doesn't.

Pointing a kernel program at a running node's data directory fails, but only because LevelDB locks `blocks/index`. To avoid a second copy of the chain, the obvious workaround is to use the node's blocks directory with the program's own data directory, or in-memory databases. It starts without error, but with an empty block index `BlockManager` writes from offset 0 of the node's `blk00000.dat`, which `FlatFileSeq::Open` opens in place with `"rb+"`. The node keeps running and serves the overwritten bytes as its own blocks.

#31674 added the blocks directory lock to bitcoind and noted that "the kernel does not currently do any dir locking, but it should". This PR follows sedited's [suggestion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31674#pullrequestreview-2560427054) to add the lock to the `BlockManager` constructor, and is based on the [`lock_blocksdir_raii`](https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/commit/e08ecc19b37b23ee936c3b14b75b3852efd1d23c) commit.

`BlockManager` holds `.lock` for its whole lifetime through `BlocksDirLock`, its first member, so the directory is locked before `xor.dat` is touched. Creating a chainstate manager on a blocks directory locked by another process, bitcoind or a kernel user, fails.

In bitcoind, init already holds the lock, so `LockDirectory` returns success without locking again. The lock is released when the `BlockManager` is destroyed rather than at exit. That happens at shutdown, and when a GUI user retries a failed chainstate load with a reindex, after which the new `BlockManager` reacquires it. A blocks directory used through the kernel now has to be writable, as bitcoind already required.

Added a regression test to feature_filelock.py.

pulls.title: Detect transaction problems early during deserialization
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521 (and not included in #36895), as it's effectively an independent improvement.

This introduces a number of additional checks that are applied during transaction deserialization, which reduce various worst case deserialization time scenarios:
* Reject transactions with more txins or more txouts than can possibly fit in a block (applied always)
* Reject transactions with 0 txins or 0 txouts (applied in P2P code only; there are RPCs like `fundrawtransaction` that explicitly support transactions with 0 inputs)

This is a mild behavior change, as detecting these problems early causes them to be treated as deserialization errors, which in P2P logic cause messages to be ignored instead of peer disconnection.

pulls.title: kernel: make btck_witness_stack_get_item_at O(1)
pulls.body:
Since #36895, `btck_witness_stack_get_item_at` walks the items before the one it returns, so reading a whole witness stack through it is O(n^2).

This keeps a span for each item in `btck_WitnessStack`, which makes `btck_witness_stack_get_item_at` O(1) without changing its signature. `btck_transaction_input_get_witness_stack` is O(n) instead of O(1), because it finds every item when it creates the witness stack.

Breaking changes:
- `btck_transaction_input_get_witness_stack` returns an owned `btck_WitnessStack*`, which must be destroyed with `btck_witness_stack_destroy`.
- The C++ wrapper's `WitnessStackView` is removed, and `GetWitnessStack()` returns a `WitnessStack`.

test: cover missing BIP352 cases
pulls.body:
The existing BIP352 tests leave several cases insufficiently covered. To identify these gaps, I ran manual mutation testing against `src/common/bip352.cpp`, complemented by `bcore-mutation`. Out of 55 mutations, 33 survived with the existing tests.

With these tests, 52 of the 55 mutations are detected. The three remaining mutations are equivalent to the original implementation.

One mutation replaces the `return std::nullopt` with `break` when `GetOp` fails while scanning a P2PKH scriptSig. The function reaches the same `return std::nullopt` after the loop. Another removes the early return for the case where there are no eligible keys, checking only whether there are no inputs. With no keys, libsecp256k1 already returns a failure, so the result remains `NOT_ELIGIBLE`. The third mutation changes the P2PKH scriptSig scanning loop condition from `pc < txin.scriptSig.end()` to `pc <= txin.scriptSig.end()`. When `pc` reaches the end of the scriptSig, `GetOp` fails, and the function returns the same `std::nullopt`.

The new tests cover scan label reporting, P2PKH public key extraction when the `scriptSig` contains unrelated pushes, invalid public keys across supported input types, P2SH-P2WPKH eligibility, Taproot script-path spends, annex handling, control block validation, prevouts summary errors, Silent Payments destination validation, label copy assignment, maximum-size control block acceptance, and the behavior of `Scan` when none of the outputs is a valid x-only key.

The existing `bip352_skips_transactions_spending_unknown_segwit_versions` test is also extended to cover SegWit versions v2 through v16 and check the exact `NOT_ELIGIBLE` error. The address decoding tests also cover a v0 address with a valid Bech32m checksum but one extra data byte (67 instead of 66). The existing `bip352_scan_skips_invalid_taproot_outputs` test is extended to verify that `Scan` returns an empty list, rather than an error, when none of the outputs is a valid x-only key.

The changes are limited to `src/test/bip352_tests.cpp`. No production code is modified.

The tests also pass on top of the P2SH changes from #36776. The annex-related mutations are detected independently of #36992.

Using `bcore-mutation` with `--one-mutant` and the `bip352_tests` test suite, the mutation score improves from 83.93% (9 of 56 mutations surviving on master) to 91.07% (5 of 56 surviving with the first PR version) and finally to 98.21% (1 of 56 surviving with this version). The only remaining survivor is the equivalent P2PKH loop-boundary mutation described above.

`src/common/bip352.cpp` is not included in the continuous mutation-testing runs on corecheck, so these gaps are not covered by those runs.

pulls.body:
`feature_torcontrol.py` can fail if the node reconnects before the test thread starts checking the backoff. This caused an intermittent CI failure on NetBSD even though the node observed the expected delay.

Record when the mock Tor server accepts the new connection and compare that timestamp with the time just before triggering the disconnect. This preserves both checks: at least half a second must have elapsed, and the node must send `PROTOCOLINFO 1` on reconnect.

On Linux, the 1.5-second delay from the issue reproduced the original failure. The updated test passed both with and without that delay.

Fixes #36934.

pulls.title: net: prevent ASMap group collisions and honor map filenames
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A mapped autonomous system and an unmapped IPv6 /32 can share an address group, so the node treats unrelated peers as part of the same network when selecting connections.
A node started with `-asmap=2026-09-asmap.dat` can also silently select the embedded map.

**Fix:** Give mapped autonomous systems their own group tag. Nodes using ASMap rebucket stored peers once on upgrade or downgrade across this change.

- Load digit-leading filenames from disk. `-asmap`, `-asmap=` and `-asmap=1` still select the embedded map. `-asmap=2` now names a file.
- Report failed path lookups as missing files, and directories or read failures as invalid maps.
- Require a new destination for `exportasmap`. A repeated export is cheap to regenerate, but exporting over a custom map silently changes what the node loads on restart. Callers reusing a path must first move or remove the file. [Original overwrite rationale](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33920#discussion_r3117087307)
- Fix the `decode --nonoverlapping` documentation and help text, and describe how `diff_addrs` groups peers by their old and new AS assignments.

---

I batched these fixes because I don't have the bandwidth to maintain several ASMap PRs. Feel free to carve out and merge individual commits. The [ASMap optimizations](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36994) can be merged independently.

pulls.title: rpc: avoid quadratic duplicate checks for unique keys in decodepsbt
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When `decodepsbt` writes partial signatures to JSON, it scans the keys it has already added for every signature.
The parser stores signatures by public key ID, so the same public key cannot appear twice in an input's signature map.

**Fix:** Append the entries directly with `pushKVEnd` to skip the repeated scans.

pulls.title: mining: handle negative and NaN wait timeouts
pulls.body:
An ipc client can pass any timeout to `waitTipChanged`, but the code assumes it is never negative:

```
Assume(timeout >= 0ms); // No internal callers should use a negative timeout
```

On debug builds, a negative or NaN timeout fails this check and aborts the node. I reproduced this with a timeout of -1.0.

On release builds the check is skipped. Negative values are clamped to zero, but NaN is not, because every comparison with NaN is false. It ends up as the deadline passed to `wait_until`.

`waitNext` has no Assume, but it also doesn't check its timeout. A NaN timeout waits one extra fee tick (about one second) before returning.

`waitTipChanged` and `waitNext` now throw an error for negative or NaN timeouts. The internal `Assume` in `WaitTipChanged` still checks internal callers. The interface documents the errors, and the functional test covers rejection of negative and NaN timeouts and acceptance of positive infinity in both methods.

I'm not aware of any client that sends these values (sv2-tp, for example, requires an interval of at least one second), so this is hardening against bad input from ipc clients.

_This is similar to #36520, which handles invalid arguments to the Chain interface for the same reason._

Links

- https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/bugs/bitcoin-2026-wait-timeout-assume/

pulls.title: net: make address overlap impossible when relaying addresses
pulls.body:
`CService::GetKey()` didn't include the network in the output. So in theory it would be possible for two IP2 and Tor addresses to have the same output from `CService::GetKey()`.

This would have unexpected results when used in the per-peer bloom filter of known addresses - we may wrongfully assume that a peer knows `foo.onion` when we have sent to them `foo.i2p`.

To make this impossible - include the network in `CService::GetKey()`.

Addrman already includes the network separately so it does not need this change. The code would be simplest if addrman also uses `GetKey()` with the network but that would mess the positions of addresses in existent databases (`peers.dat`). So, keep a variant of network-less `GetKey()` for addrman.

Thanks, @l0rinc for pointing me into this. I think it is minor but also the change is minor, so worth fixing IMO.

pulls.title: p2p: Use separate compact block nonce per network
pulls.body:
This issue was reported by ajtowns on IRC some time ago.

For compact blocks, when we serve the last compact block from cache, we use a single nonce for all peers currently.
This means anyone can request the most recent tip as a compact block via `getdata(MSG_CMPCT_BLOCK)` over a clearnet and a tor connection and then compare the nonces - if they match it's the same node.

Fix this by using a different nonce per network/bind (`CNode::m_network_key`). 
This means a little bit more work in `NewPoWValidBlock` where we will now create `CBlockHeaderAndShortTxIDs` objects for each network on which a peer has made us their hb peer. More instances may be created later when serving non-hb peers via `GETDATA`. Note that while on master, the `CBlockHeaderAndShortTxIDs` was created eagerly, and its serialization lazily, we now create both objects lazily.

From a high-level point of view, there are various remaining fingerprinting vectors even with this fix, some hard to fix, but I do think that we should be fixing at least the most obvious ones.

pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block and undo writers rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the last buffered bytes.
If the filesystem fills up, `fwrite()` can write fewer bytes than requested (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
When this happens during the final flush, `AutoFile::write_buffer()` throws and the exception escapes the implicitly non-throwing destructor, invoking `std::terminate` before the node can report the write error and shut down normally.
Adding an explicit `flush()` alone would still leave the same bytes pending on failure, so the destructor would retry the write during unwinding.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly. If serialization or flushing throws `std::ios_base::failure`, they call `discard()` to drop any pending bytes, log the error, close the file, and request shutdown.

`BufferedWriter::flush()` clears the pending byte count before calling `write_buffer()` and propagates any exception. Retrying would be unsafe because the stream may have obfuscated the bytes in place and a short write may already have put some of them on disk.
The destructor uses `Assume` to check that no bytes are pending before its fallback flush.

<details>
<summary>Manual write-error reproducer</summary>

Force `AutoFile::write_buffer()` to report a write failure even when `fwrite()` succeeds.

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, flushing from the destructor invokes `std::terminate`.

```text
libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::__1::ios_base::failure: AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
zsh: abort      build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"
exit=134
```

With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure, completes normal shutdown, and exits with status 1.

```text
Checking all blk files are present...
[error] Failed to write block file FlatFilePos(nFile=0, nPos=8): AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
...
Error: A fatal internal error occurred, see debug.log for details: Failed to write block.
[error] Writing genesis block to disk failed
[error] Error initializing block database
...
Shutdown done
exit=1
```
</details>

pulls.title: wallet: fix negative bump fees after clearing a coin selection
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `SelectionResult::Clear()` removes the selected inputs but keeps their bump fee discount. `GetTotalBumpFees()` then subtracts that discount from zero, so any positive discount gives the empty selection a negative fee total. The wallet currently avoids this because it only clears selections inside the knapsack solver, before applying the discount.

**Fix:** Reset the discount along with the inputs it applies to.

pulls.title: contrib: require trusted signers in verify.py
pulls.body:
`verify_shasums_signature` previously separated signatures into `good_trusted` and `good_untrusted`, but computed `num_trusted = len(good_trusted) + len(good_untrusted)` (and added all `expired` entries under `--allow-expired`). As a result, valid signatures from untrusted keys present in the local GPG keyring satisfied `--min-good-sigs` even when none of them were trusted in GPG or matched `--trusted-keys`.

In addition, `README.md` documents passing full 40-character primary key fingerprints to `--trusted-keys`, whereas `parse_gpg_result` only recorded the key identifier from `GOODSIG`/`EXPKEYSIG` and ignored `VALIDSIG` fingerprints, and did not deduplicate multiple signatures from the same primary key.

Changes:
- Count only distinct, non-revoked trusted signers toward `--min-good-sigs` (including under `--allow-expired`) directly in the signature loop.
- Parse signing and primary key fingerprints from GnuPG `VALIDSIG` status lines so `--trusted-keys` matches full fingerprints while deduplicating by primary key fingerprint.
- Clarify `--trusted-keys` and signer counting in `contrib/verify-binaries/README.md`.
- Extend `test_inactive_signature_quorum` in `contrib/verify-binaries/test.py`.

pulls.title: blockstorage: fix partial-mask assertions and genesis availability checks
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `CheckBlockDataAvailability` checks whether the upper block has any requested bit. `GetFirstBlock` requires every requested bit, so a partial match can reach its assertion. At genesis, the existing undo exception can reject an undo-only request or accept a request with missing block data. It also misses ranges containing only genesis.

**Fix:** Require every requested bit on each block in the range, except that genesis needs no undo data. An empty mask now succeeds for a valid range because it requests no bits. Both index-startup calls supply nonempty masks.

pulls.title: rpc: Use OBJ_NAMED_PARAMS in estimatesmartfee
pulls.body:
`estimatesmartfee` is the only RPC that rejects named arguments for options, which seems confusing and not user friendly.

Fix it by using `OBJ_NAMED_PARAMS`.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240
